submission.natural_language_explanation: L5/N428+ is a sentence-onset lexical detector: it fires on the first word of a new sentence - the content word that begins immediately after a sentence boundary (a period, question mark, or a paragraph/line break), with the peak usually inside that first word's sub-tokens (e.g. ' Resorption', ' Gait', ' Practitioners', ' Milk'). It is near zero on the boundary punctuation itself, on the same content word when it sits mid-sentence or after a comma, and on sentences that open with a pronoun, determiner or discourse connective (' It', ' The', ' However'); across the scan, sentence-onset content words average 0.57 with 25% above 1.0, versus 0.18 for sentence-onset function words and -0.08 for every other token.

Navigation in the eighteenth century depended on a problem that no instrument could solve. Sailors could measure latitude easily enough, but longitude required knowing the time at a fixed reference point to within a few seconds. Pendulum clocks lost minutes on a rolling deck, and the oils that lubricated their gears thickened in cold weather.

John Harrison spent forty years building clocks that might survive a voyage. His fourth machine, a large watch rather than a pendulum clock, was carried to Jamaica in 1761 and performed far better than anyone had expected. Astronomers who examined the results refused to believe them at first. Rival candidates, including the lunar distance method championed by the Astronomer Royal, had powerful supporters in Parliament.

The argument dragged on for decades, and Harrison received most of his reward only after appealing directly to the King. A second voyage tested a copy of the watch under harder conditions. Cook carried one on his second circumnavigation and reported that it kept time well enough to fix his position after months at sea. Copies became standard equipment on naval vessels within a generation.

Ordinary merchant captains were slower to adopt the new instruments. Expense was one obstacle, and suspicion of the astronomers was another. Training officers to wind and rate a chronometer took weeks, and a single mistake could ruin a run of observations. Nevertheless, the demand for accurate charts grew as trade expanded, and the instruments spread through the fleets of every maritime nation.

By the middle of the nineteenth century, a ship without a chronometer was considered unfit for long voyages. Insurance underwriters began to ask whether one was aboard before they would quote a rate. The device that Harrison had hidden behind panels and explained only reluctantly had become an ordinary piece of professional equipment.
